record.question:
A company runs MySQL on EC2 in us-east-1 and has a prepared application fleet in us-west-2. It wants a managed database design for Regional disaster recovery with a target RPO below 1 minute and target application RTO below 5 minutes. The company can migrate to a MySQL-compatible engine. The recovery procedure must make a secondary database writable and reconnect the application.

Which design provides the strongest fit for these objectives?

options.text: Migrate to RDS for MySQL and create a cross-Region read replica. During an outage, change application DNS to the replica endpoint without promoting the replica.

Migrate to Aurora MySQL Global Database with a provisioned secondary cluster in us-west-2. Monitor replication lag and automate a tested cross-Region failover procedure, application reconnection, and traffic redirection.
Migrate to an RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance in us-east-1 and rely on its standby for a complete us-east-1 outage.
Copy daily database snapshots to us-west-2. During an outage, restore the newest snapshot and manually reconfigure the application.

explanation.text:
<<2>> maintains a cross-Region database through Aurora Global Database storage-level replication and includes the steps needed to resume writes. AWS describes typical unplanned-failover RPO in seconds and recovery time in minutes, making this a strong design candidate. Validate the complete application recovery time, including detection, failover, connections and traffic switching, against the stated targets.

<<1>> leaves the RDS replica read-only; DNS alone does not promote it. A properly promoted and tested RDS replica can support other DR designs, but this procedure is incomplete. <<3>> provides AZ resilience inside one Region, not a secondary Region. <<4>> can lose up to the snapshot interval of changes and adds restore and manual reconfiguration time.

Cross-Region replication is asynchronous. Actual data loss depends on lag at failure, and neither a service name nor a nominal failover duration guarantees the application’s RPO or RTO.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-global-database-disaster-recovery.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/AuroraMySQL.Replication.CrossRegion.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html

diagram_alt: The recovery sequence distinguishes replication lag from all the steps that determine application downtime.

sources.supports: Unplanned Global Database failover, lag-dependent RPO and recovery in minutes.
Global Database uses Aurora storage-layer replication rather than MySQL binlog replication.
Read replicas require promotion to become standalone writable databases.

editorial_notes: Made the RDS replica distractor specifically incomplete instead of claiming RDS cross-Region replicas can never meet such targets.
